rows.question: How did our carriers' on-time performance change in Q3, especially on reefer?
rows.answer: All-loads on-time pickup slipped in Q3 2026 to 93.1% from 95.4% in Q2, and on-time delivery fell to 91.8% from 94.0% [1][2]. Reefer was the weakest mode: on-time delivery dropped to 87.2% from 92.5%, and carrier fall-offs on reefer loads more than doubled to 4.4% from 2.1% [3][4]. The scorecard attributes the reefer slide to a September hurricane and longer produce dwell times, and the market memo confirms Hurricane Corinne stranded roughly 1,100 refrigerated trailers, while tender acceptance on Southeast reefer fell to 78% in September [5][6][7]. Produce detention rose to $41,800 in September from $23,500 in June, and only 62% was billed back to shippers because signed BOL in/out times were missing [8][9]. The pricing desk recommends reopening Q4 rates with the top 20 produce shippers, adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge, and booking holiday produce 72 hours ahead [10].

rows.answer: Southeast retail diesel averaged $3.94 per gallon in the week of October 6, 2026, up 31 cents from $3.63 at the start of July [1][2]. A typical broker table that adds one cent per mile for every six-cent diesel rise would put the 31-cent increase at roughly five cents more per mile in fuel surcharge [2]. Caveat: the only price source is Gulf Fuel Watch, which labels itself a fictional demo document with invented prices [4], so these figures must be confirmed against an official series and against Ridgeline's own surcharge table before anyone acts on them. For reefer lanes, our pricing desk recommends adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge line, and a reefer unit burns roughly 0.8 gallons of diesel per hour while cooling [3][5].

rows.question: Summarize the broker transparency rule and what Ridgeline must change.
rows.answer: The broker transparency final rule requires a property broker to keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years, including shipper payment, carrier payment, and accessorial charges, and to deliver that record electronically within 48 hours when a party to the transaction asks [1][2][3]. It bans contract clauses in which carriers waive their right to see the transaction record, and the rule takes effect February 1, 2027; the August 1, 2027 date applies only to brokers with fewer than 10 employees, which does not fit Ridgeline's 140 staff [4][5][6]. Non-compliance on the 48-hour window can bring a fine of up to $10,000 per violation and, for repeat violations, suspension of operating authority [7]. For Ridgeline this means removing waiver clauses from carrier agreements, making the TMS store shipper and carrier payment amounts on the same load record, and building a request process that can produce records within 48 hours [4][8]. Caveat: all rule terms come from one secondary digest, not the official rule text, so verify against the Federal Register or FMCSA before acting [1][7].

rows.question: Under the food traceability requirement, what do we as a broker have to keep or provide on produce loads?
rows.answer: Under the food traceability requirement, the record-keeping duty for produce on the traceability list (fresh tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens, melons, fresh-cut fruit) sits mainly with shippers and receivers, who must record the traceability lot code, quantity, and origin and destination for each shipment [1][2]. As a broker that only transports the food, Ridgeline is not required to keep traceability lot codes, but it must be able to produce shipping documents within 24 hours when a shipper or receiver requests them during a recall [1][3]. Temperature logs are not required by the rule, although receivers may make continuous reefer logs a contract condition [4].

rows.question: What did the fall carrier survey say about reefer carriers shrinking or leaving the market, and why?
rows.answer: The fall 2026 Mid-South Carrier Pulse Survey found that 22% of reefer carriers plan to reduce fleet size within six months, and 9% are considering leaving reefer for dry van [1]. Carriers planning to shrink cited insurance premiums (64%), equipment financing costs (51%), and unpaid detention time (47%) as the main reasons [2]; the survey also found only 11% plan to add trucks [3] and that Forty-one percent of reefer carriers refuse loads from at least one shipper because of chronic detention [4]. For Ridgeline, this matches our own data: the Southeast lost an estimated 6% of small reefer fleets since January, mostly owner-operators with one to five trucks [5], our reefer cancellations after acceptance rose to 4.4% in Q3 from 2.1% in Q2 [6], and contract tender acceptance on Southeast reefer fell to 78% in September [7].

rows.answer: Per the one 2027 source in the library, five of the largest LTL carriers have announced early-2027 general rate increases ranging from 4.9% to 6.5%, with a median of 5.9% [1]. rows.question: What's driving reefer spot rates out of the Southeast this quarter, and what does it mean for our produce shippers?
rows.answer: Southeast reefer spot rates averaged $2.87 per mile in Q3, up 14% from Q2, driven by a produce season that ran three weeks long, Hurricane Corinne closing the Port of Savannah, and a shrinking small-carrier reefer fleet [1][2][3][4]. Capacity stays tight because only 11% of reefer carriers plan to add trucks and 41% refuse loads from at least one shipper over chronic detention [5][6]. For our produce shippers, spring contract rates now sit well below market and our Southeast reefer tender acceptance fell to 78% in September, so more of their loads are going to spot at higher cost [7][8]. Ridgeline's market memo expects Southeast reefer spot to ease to $2.60 to $2.70 per mile in Q4, and recommends reopening Q4 contract rates with our top 20 produce shippers rather than waiting for the January bid [9][10].
